title: Overfitting and underfitting
story:
The error you can measure most easily is the one that tells you least. Training error falls monotonically as a model gains capacity — give it enough and it reaches zero, by memorising. A quantity that always improves when you add parameters cannot tell you when to stop adding them.

What is diagnostic is the relationship between two errors rather than the value of either. Plot training error and held-out error against capacity and there are two regimes. While capacity is too low, both are high and both fall together: the model cannot express the structure that is there, and more capacity helps on seen and unseen data alike. That is underfitting, and its signature is that training error is bad. Past some point the two separate: training error keeps falling while held-out error turns and rises. The model is now fitting things specific to the sample it was given. That is overfitting, and its signature is the gap rather than either number alone.

Geman, Bienenstock and Doursat gave the underlying account in 1992, treating feedforward networks trained by error backpropagation as nonparametric regression estimators and showing that estimation error decomposes into two distinct components. Large numbers of parameter estimates raise the variance, whereas incorrect statistical models increase the bias. Those are the two regimes in their proper terms, and the next lesson takes the decomposition seriously.

What matters practically is that the two failures need opposite remedies, so misdiagnosis is expensive. Underfitting calls for more capacity, better features, a less restrictive model, less regularisation. Overfitting calls for the reverse — less capacity, more regularisation, more data, fewer features. Apply the wrong one and you move further from the answer with every iteration while apparently working hard, which is why the diagnosis should come before the intervention rather than after two weeks of tuning.

One caution about received wisdom here. The account above is the classical one and it is the right default for the methods in this track, where it describes what you will actually see. It is not a universal law: very large modern models are routinely trained well past the point of interpolating their training data and do not behave the way this curve predicts. That is an active area rather than a settled one, and the honest position is that the classical picture governs the regime this track is about, not every regime there is.

problem.name: Capacity diagnosis
problem.shape: A model's performance on unseen data is worse than wanted, and the fix depends on which of two opposite causes is responsible.
tell: training error is near zero and held-out error is not
both errors are high and close together
held-out error started rising while training error kept falling
someone is tuning without having looked at both errors
problem.move: Measure both errors before changing anything. If both are high, the model lacks capacity or the features lack signal — add capacity, add features, regularise less. If training error is low and held-out error is much higher, do the reverse. Track the two as capacity varies rather than inspecting a single point.
problem.invariant: Training error falls monotonically with capacity and cannot indicate when to stop. The diagnostic quantity is the relationship between training and held-out error, not the value of either.
problem.breaks: The two-regime picture describes the classical setting this track occupies and is not a universal law — very large models are routinely trained past the point of interpolating their training data without behaving as the curve predicts, so the diagnosis is reliable here and should not be exported wholesale.

cost.time: fitting across a range of capacities rather than at one setting, which is the cost of having a diagnosis instead of a guess
cost.space: held-out data, permanently withheld from fitting
cost.beats: tuning by held-out score alone, which tells you that something is wrong without telling you in which direction to move

worked.problem: What can training error alone tell you?
worked.reasoning:
Very little, and the reason is structural rather than practical.

Training error falls monotonically as capacity increases. Add parameters and it goes down; add enough and it reaches zero, because the model can memorise. So a low training error is compatible with an excellent model and with a useless one, and the quantity cannot distinguish them. Any measure that always improves when you add capacity cannot tell you when to stop adding capacity.

There is exactly one thing it does tell you, and it is worth having. A high training error is informative: it means the model cannot fit the data it was shown, which rules out overfitting entirely and points at insufficient capacity, features without signal, or an optimisation that has not converged. That is a genuine diagnosis, and it is the case where you should add rather than subtract.

Everything else requires the second measurement. With both errors you get a direction rather than just a verdict. Both high and close: underfitting — more capacity, better features, less regularisation. Training low and held-out much higher: overfitting — less capacity, more regularisation, more data, fewer features. The gap is the diagnostic, not either number.

Why this matters more than it sounds: the two remedies are opposites. Misdiagnose and every iteration moves you further from the answer while feeling like progress, which is how weeks get spent regularising a model that needed more capacity.

I would add two qualifications rather than leave the rule bare. The first is that a single pair of numbers is weaker than the curve — watching both errors across a range of capacities shows you where they separate, which is the information you actually wanted. The second is about scope: this two-regime picture is the classical account, it is the right default for the methods in this track, and it is not a universal law. Very large models are routinely trained past the point of interpolating their training data and do not follow the curve. The honest statement is that this describes the regime we are in here, and I would not export it further than that.

problem.practice: Fit one model family across a range of capacities — tree depth, or polynomial degree — and plot training and held-out error together against that range. Find where the curves separate. Then take a model you are currently tuning and check which side of that point it is on before making another change.

beats.broke: The only error you can measure directly is the error on data you already have, and that quantity falls monotonically as the model gains capacity, so it cannot tell you when to stop.
beats.fix: Watch the two errors separately. Training and held-out error move together while capacity is too low and apart once it is too high, and the point where they separate is what you were looking for.
beats.cost: The diagnosis requires held-out data and therefore costs data, and the two failures need opposite remedies — so misreading which one you have makes matters actively worse.

interview.q: What can training error alone tell you?
interview.trap: Treating a low training error as evidence of a good model. It is compatible with an excellent model and with pure memorisation, and cannot separate them — though a high training error is genuinely informative, since it rules out overfitting.
interview.answer:
Very little, for a structural reason.

Training error falls monotonically as capacity increases, reaching zero once the model can memorise. So a low training error is equally consistent with an excellent model and a useless one, and any measure that always improves when you add capacity cannot tell you when to stop adding it.

There is one thing it does tell you, and it is worth having: a high training error is informative. It means the model cannot fit even the data it was shown, which rules out overfitting and points instead at insufficient capacity, features carrying no signal, or an optimisation that has not converged. That is a real diagnosis, and it is the case where you add rather than subtract.

Everything else needs the second measurement, and with both you get a direction rather than a verdict. Both high and close together means underfitting — more capacity, better features, less regularisation. Training low with held-out much higher means overfitting — less capacity, more regularisation, more data, fewer features. The gap is the diagnostic, not either number alone.

This matters because the remedies are opposites: misdiagnose and each iteration moves you further from the answer while feeling productive, which is how weeks get spent regularising a model that needed more capacity.

Two qualifications. A single pair of numbers is weaker than the curve — watching both errors across a range of capacities shows where they separate, which is the information actually wanted. And this two-regime picture is the classical account: it is the right default for these methods and it is not universal, since very large models are routinely trained past interpolating their training data without following the curve. I would not export it beyond the regime it describes.
